title: Yellow eyes in a 78-year-old retired welder
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination in general practice of a 78-year-old retired welder with more than a month of deepening jaundice, tea-coloured urine, pale stools, a mild epigastric ache radiating to the back, anorexia, weight loss and lethargy. He had a cholecystectomy 10 years ago, developed type 2 diabetes 3 years ago and has smoked since he was 15. He wonders whether his wife's carrot juice is to blame. The candidate then interprets his blood tests, tumour marker, hepatitis serology and a pancreatic-protocol CT, recognises obstructive jaundice from a suspected pancreatic head cancer, refers him urgently through the optimal care pathway, explains the results and gives safety-netting advice.
focus: Recognising obstructive jaundice with red flags for pancreatic cancer in an older patient, and arranging urgent referral from general practice
presentation: Epigastric pain radiating to the back
stem: You are a medical student on placement at a general practice in Williamstown, Melbourne. Jake Morrison, a 78-year-old retired welder, has come in at his wife's insistence because of yellowing of his eyes. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Morrison and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Morrison's blood tests, tumour marker and hepatitis serology, and his CT scan report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jake Morrison, a 78-year-old retired welder. You are relaxed and a bit matter-of-fact; you only came because your wife Barbara insisted. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I noticed some yellowing in my eyes, and my wife told me to come in and have it checked."

The yellowing (give only when asked):

  • "I can't really remember when it came on... it must have been a while, definitely over a month." It has never happened to you before.
  • It is there all the time and may be getting darker. "This morning when I was getting ready, I thought to myself that it must have gotten worse. My wife said so too."
  • "It doesn't bother me much."

Tummy pain (only if asked about pain):

  • A dull ache in the middle of your upper tummy, just under the rib cage.
  • You thought it was reflux, but antacids didn't help.
  • Only if asked: about 3 out of 10, and it goes through to your back.

Urine (only if asked): "Yes, now you've mentioned it, my urine has been quite dark for the past while. It's like the colour of tea." No burning, frequency or blood.

Stools (only if asked specifically about colour): they have been paler, a bit washed out.

Systemic symptoms (only if asked):

  • Poor appetite: "That's why my wife is making me drink juices."
  • Weight loss: "My pants are a little baggy now." You haven't weighed yourself.
  • You've been more tired and lethargic.
  • No fevers, sweats or shivers.

Say no to all of these if asked: itch, nausea, vomiting, a swollen tummy, vomiting blood or black stools, recent travel, tattoos, blood transfusions, needle-stick injuries.

Past medical history:

  • High blood pressure and high cholesterol.
  • Type 2 diabetes, diagnosed 3 years ago.
  • Inguinal hernia repair 5 years ago.
  • Gallbladder removed by keyhole surgery 10 years ago.
  • Only if asked: you have never had hepatitis, any other liver problems or kidney disease.

Medications: metformin, atorvastatin and perindopril. You also take a magnesium aspartate supplement. Nothing new recently.

Drugs (only if asked): you tried cocaine a few times when you were young, never injected anything.

Vaccinations: "Not sure, to be honest."

Allergies: cefazolin (an antibiotic given at one of your operations) gave you a rash.

Family history: your mother died at about 90 of kidney failure. Your father died of a heart attack in his 70s. No blood disorders in the family. No one in the family has had cancer of the pancreas, bowel or liver, as far as you know.

Social history:

  • Smoking: half a pack a day from age 15; you have cut down to 3 or 4 a day now.
  • Alcohol: a social drinker. If asked to put a number on it: a couple of beers with friends at the weekend.
  • You worked as a welder for 40 years and are now retired. You used to walk to work; now you do the gardening and the shopping.
  • You eat balanced meals.
  • You live with your wife Barbara in a unit in Williamstown. You have three sons: two live overseas and one lives in Melbourne and visits.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "Is it because of my diet? My wife has been making me drink carrot juices lately."
  • Concerns: you are not worried yourself, but Barbara and your son in Melbourne seem worried.
  • Expectations: you would like to know what it is so Barbara will stop fussing.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Is it the carrot juice?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: slim older man whose clothes look loose, alert and comfortable, visibly jaundiced. No scratch marks. Weight 68 kg, height 176 cm. Practice records: 75 kg eight months ago.
  • Observations: temperature 36.8 °C, HR 82 regular, BP 134/80, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, capillary BGL 13.4 mmol/L (random).
  • Hands: no clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema or Dupuytren's contracture. No asterixis. Nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers.
  • Eyes and face: scleral icterus. Conjunctivae slightly pale. No xanthelasma.
  • Neck: no left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node or cervical lymphadenopathy.
  • Chest: no spider naevi or gynaecomastia. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. Healed laparoscopic port scars and a right inguinal scar. No periumbilical nodule.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft, mild tenderness in the epigastrium, no guarding. No palpable mass. Liver edge not palpable; liver span normal to percussion. No splenomegaly. No palpable gallbladder. Murphy's sign negative.
  • Ascites: shifting dullness negative.
  • Legs: no oedema, calves soft and non-tender.
  • Rectal examination (if offered with a chaperone): pale, clay-coloured stool on the glove, no blood or melaena, no mass.
  • Urine dipstick (if requested): bilirubin 3+, urobilinogen negative, glucose 2+, no blood, leucocytes or nitrites.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms Jake's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language, takes his carrot-juice idea seriously without dismissing it, and acknowledges that his wife and family are worried.
History
Characterises the jaundice:

kids.x: Onset and duration: yellow eyes, came on gradually over more than a month, never happened before.
Course: present all the time and getting darker, worse this morning, noticed by his wife.

check.x: Asks about urine colour: dark, tea-coloured urine for some time, with no urinary symptoms.
Asks specifically about stool colour: paler, less pigmented stools.
check.d: Jake only volunteers this when asked specifically about stool colour.

check.x: Characterises the abdominal pain: dull central ache under the rib cage, 3/10, radiating to the back, thought to be reflux and not relieved by antacids.
Asks about other gastrointestinal and cholangitis symptoms: itch, nausea, vomiting, distension, fever, sweats or rigors (all absent).
check.d: Award for itch plus at least two others.

check.x: Asks about constitutional symptoms: poor appetite, weight loss (trousers baggy) and lethargy.
Takes the past medical and surgical history:

kids.x: Hypertension, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes diagnosed only 3 years ago (at 75).
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy 10 years ago and inguinal hernia repair 5 years ago.
No known hepatitis, liver or kidney disease.

check.x: Asks about liver and hepatitis risk factors: injecting drug use (none; cocaine a few times when young), alcohol quantified, travel (none), transfusions or tattoos (none), and hepatitis vaccination (unsure).
check.d: Award for at least three risk factors, including alcohol quantified.

check.x: Takes a medication history including supplements and recent changes: metformin, atorvastatin, perindopril and magnesium aspartate, nothing new.
Asks about allergies and the reaction: cefazolin caused a rash.
Takes a family history: mother died at about 90 of kidney failure, father died of a heart attack in his 70s, no blood disorders, and asks about pancreatic, bowel or liver cancer in the family.
check.d: Award for asking about family history of cancer, including pancreatic, bowel or liver cancer; details of parents' deaths not required.

check.x: Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified: half a pack a day from age 15, now 3 to 4 a day.
Welder for 40 years, now retired; active with gardening and shopping.
Lives with his wife Barbara in a unit in Williamstown; three sons, one in Melbourne who visits.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders about the carrot juice, is not bothered himself, but his wife and son are worried.
Examination
Asks for vital signs including temperature (afebrile), and weighs him against previous records (75 kg to 68 kg in eight months).
Checks a capillary blood glucose given his diabetes (13.4 mmol/L, random).
Inspects generally: jaundiced with scleral icterus, slim with loose clothes, no scratch marks, slightly pale conjunctivae.
Looks for signs of chronic liver disease: clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia and asterixis (none present).
check.d: Award for at least four signs.

check.x: Palpates for the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node and cervical lymph nodes.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspects: laparoscopic port and inguinal scars, no distension.
Palpates all regions: mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding or mass.
Palpates for the liver, spleen and gallbladder, and notes that a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign) cannot be expected after cholecystectomy.
kids.d: Credit the Courvoisier point whenever it is made.

kids.x: Checks for ascites (shifting dullness) and a periumbilical nodule.

check.x: Offers a rectal examination with a chaperone (pale stool) and requests a urine dipstick (bilirubin 3+, urobilinogen negative, glycosuria).

Summarises the findings as an obstructive (post-hepatic) picture: jaundice with dark urine, pale stools and weight loss, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, and raises concern about a malignant cause.
Interpretation
Interprets the LFTs as cholestatic: bilirubin 186 (mostly conjugated) with ALP 612 and GGT 845 raised far more than ALT 142 and AST 98, fitting biliary obstruction.
Interprets INR 1.4 as likely vitamin K malabsorption from biliary obstruction rather than liver failure, and notes it matters before any procedure.

Interprets the other bloods: mild normocytic anaemia, normal white cells and only mildly raised CRP in an afebrile patient (no evidence of cholangitis now), adequate renal function, normal lipase, and HbA1c risen from 6.6% to 8.4% (worsening diabetes, which fits pancreatic cancer).
check.d: Award for at least three of these.

check.x: Interprets the serology: no hepatitis B or C (and not immune to hepatitis B); CA 19-9 of 1,240 is markedly raised and supports pancreatic cancer but is not diagnostic, because biliary obstruction alone can raise it.
check.d: Award for negative viral hepatitis serology plus CA 19-9 described as supportive but not diagnostic; hepatitis B immunity status not required.

check.x: Interprets the CT: 32 mm hypoattenuating pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign (dilated CBD and pancreatic duct), no stone, no liver or peritoneal metastases and no arterial or venous involvement, so it appears resectable on imaging, pending staging.
check.d: Award for pancreatic head mass with double duct sign, plus no metastases and vessels clear (appears resectable).

check.x: Gives suspected pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing obstructive jaundice as the most likely diagnosis, justified by the history (progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pain to the back, weight loss, smoking, recent-onset diabetes) and the results.

Gives at least three differentials with a feature for or against each: distal cholangiocarcinoma or ampullary cancer, a common bile duct stone, a benign post-cholecystectomy stricture, intrahepatic cholestasis (drug-induced or viral hepatitis), carotenaemia.
check.d: Award for at least three with a feature for or against.

check.x: Management

Refers urgently via the optimal care pathway to a hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgical unit with a pancreatic multidisciplinary team: involves the supervising GP, phones the registrar, and sends a letter with the results and his cefazolin allergy.
check.d: Award for urgent referral to the hepatobiliary and pancreatic team or MDT by phone to the registrar, plus a letter or results sent; the allergy and the GP's involvement add to it but are not essential.

check.x: Outlines what the specialist team will do: staging CT of the chest, endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy for a tissue diagnosis, MDT discussion of surgery and chemotherapy, and biliary stenting by ERCP if needed (for example for cholangitis, itch or delayed surgery).
Gives a warning shot, then explains in plain words: a growth in the pancreas blocking the bile duct, very likely cancer, biopsy needed; does not promise an operation.
check.d: Extra credit for checking his understanding and that he is happy for Barbara to hear; not required.

check.x: Answers the carrot-juice question: carrots can tint the skin but not the whites of the eyes, and they did not cause this.
check.d: Credit whether answered in Part 1 or Part 2.

check.x: Mentions GP support: glucose review, dietitian or enzymes, quit support, Cancer Council 13 11 20 (award for any one).
Safety netting
Tells him to go to the ED (or call 000 if very unwell) for fever, shivers or shakes, worsening tummy pain, confusion or drowsiness, vomiting blood or black stools.
check.d: Award for fever or rigors plus at least two others, linked to the ED or 000.

check.x: Tells him to get same-day GP or ED review for a swollen or painful leg, and to call 000 for sudden breathlessness or chest pain.
Tells him to see the GP sooner if he keeps vomiting, cannot eat, develops a bad itch, or has very high sugar readings with thirst and passing a lot of urine.
Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week, confirms the specialist appointment date and asks him to call if he has not heard within a few days, and gives written information.
check.d: Award for a GP review within a week plus a plan to chase the specialist appointment if not heard within a few days; written information is not required.

part2.lead: Jake had blood tests on the day you first saw him, and your supervising GP arranged an urgent pancreatic-protocol CT two days later. He has come back today with his wife Barbara for the results. Jake and Barbara are in the waiting room while you call the registrar; they come back in for Question 3. Here are his results.
part2.patient:
Jake and Barbara come back in from the waiting room for Question 3. Jake is quiet and calm. Ask these once each during Question 3:

  • "Are you telling me it's cancer?"
  • "Will they be able to operate?"

If told it is probably cancer, pause, then say: "I suppose I'd better ring the boys." If the candidate uses jargon such as "obstructive", "MDT" or "ERCP" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at the practice on the day of the first visit.
handover.model:
• Read: bilirubin 186, mostly conjugated, with ALP 612 and GGT 845 raised far more than ALT 142 and AST 98: a cholestatic pattern. INR 1.4, albumin 32. Mild normocytic anaemia (Hb 118). White cells normal, CRP 9. Renal function adequate (eGFR 66). Lipase normal. HbA1c 8.4%, up from 6.6% a year ago.
  • For Jake: conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a cholestatic pattern fits biliary obstruction, as do the dark urine and pale stools. The INR most likely reflects vitamin K malabsorption, because bile is not reaching the gut, rather than liver failure. He is afebrile with normal white cells, so there is no evidence of cholangitis now. Worsening diabetes alongside weight loss in an older smoker raises concern about pancreatic cancer.
  • What it changes: it confirms an obstructive cause, which needs urgent imaging and referral. The INR needs correcting before any procedure, as the team directs.

handover.label: Tumour marker and hepatitis serology
handover.result: Same sample. Laboratory comment: CA 19-9 may be raised in biliary obstruction and cholangitis without malignancy; interpret with clinical and imaging findings.
handover.model:
• Read: CA 19-9 1,240 U/mL, more than 30 times the upper limit. HBsAg, anti-HBc, hepatitis C antibody and hepatitis A IgM all not detected; anti-HBs below 10.
  • For Jake: no viral hepatitis, so hepatitis is not the cause of the jaundice. He is not immune to hepatitis B. A CA 19-9 this high supports a pancreatic or biliary cancer, but it is not diagnostic, because biliary obstruction alone can raise it, and some people do not make CA 19-9 at all.
  • What it changes: it is a baseline for the specialist team to follow after biliary drainage and treatment. It does not replace a tissue diagnosis. Hepatitis B vaccination can be offered later; it is not a priority now.

rows.n: may be raised by biliary obstruction

handover.label: CT abdomen and pelvis (pancreatic protocol)
handover.result:
Examination: CT abdomen and pelvis, pancreatic protocol, with IV contrast (non-contrast, pancreatic phase and portal venous phase).

Clinical details: 78-year-old man with more than a month of progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, epigastric pain radiating to the back and weight loss. Cholecystectomy 10 years ago. Type 2 diabetes. Bilirubin 186, ALP 612.

Comparison: none available.

Findings:

  • Pancreas: an ill-defined hypoattenuating mass in the pancreatic head measuring 32 x 28 mm. The main pancreatic duct is dilated upstream to 6 mm, with atrophy of the pancreatic body and tail.
  • Bile ducts: the common bile duct is dilated to 14 mm and ends abruptly at the mass (double duct sign). There is moderate intrahepatic biliary dilatation. No bile duct calculus.
  • Gallbladder: surgically absent.
  • Vessels: no contact with the superior mesenteric artery, coeliac axis or common hepatic artery. The superior mesenteric vein and portal vein are patent, with a preserved fat plane from the mass.
  • Liver: no focal lesion.
  • Lymph nodes: a 9 mm peripancreatic node, not enlarged by size criteria. No other lymphadenopathy.
  • Peritoneum: no ascites or peritoneal nodularity.
  • Other: lung bases clear. Spleen, adrenals and kidneys unremarkable. Healed right inguinal hernia repair.

Conclusion: pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign, highly suspicious for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. No distant metastases on this study, and no vascular involvement, so it appears resectable on imaging.
handover.model:
• Read: a 32 mm hypoattenuating pancreatic head mass with abrupt cut-off of a dilated CBD (14 mm) and pancreatic duct (6 mm), the double duct sign, with intrahepatic duct dilatation and body and tail atrophy. No stone seen. No liver or peritoneal metastases; a 9 mm peripancreatic node, not enlarged by size criteria. No arterial or venous involvement.
  • For Jake: this confirms extrahepatic (post-hepatic) biliary obstruction from a mass in the head of the pancreas, most likely pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The duct ending at a mass argues strongly against choledocholithiasis; no stone is seen, though CT can miss stones. A mass centred in the pancreatic head with pancreatic duct dilatation favours pancreatic cancer over a distal cholangiocarcinoma, though ampullary and distal bile duct cancers can look similar.
  • What it changes: it appears resectable on imaging, so time matters. He needs urgent referral to a hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgical unit, a staging CT of the chest, a tissue diagnosis by endoscopic ultrasound, and MDT discussion. Surgery is the only potentially curative treatment.

ask: You are now calling the hepatobiliary surgical registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jake Morrison, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jake now, here in general practice.
Before Jake goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student with the GP, practice; Jake Morrison, 78.
  • Situation: obstructive jaundice with a pancreatic head mass on CT, suspected pancreatic cancer; requesting urgent review.
  • Background: more than a month of jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, epigastric pain to the back, 7 kg weight loss. Cholecystectomy 10 years ago, T2DM for 3 years, long-term smoker. Cefazolin allergy (rash).
  • Assessment: afebrile, stable. Bilirubin 186 (conjugated), ALP 612, GGT 845: cholestatic. INR 1.4, likely vitamin K malabsorption. HbA1c up to 8.4%. CA 19-9 1,240. Hepatitis serology negative. CT: 32 mm head mass, double duct sign, no metastases, vessels clear.
  • Recommendation: urgent outpatient review this week for staging, EUS biopsy and MDT; advice on biliary drainage and vitamin K.

Most likely: pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing obstructive jaundice. Progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pain radiating to the back, anorexia, weight loss, smoking, diabetes from age 75; cholestatic LFTs, CA 19-9 1,240, head mass with double duct sign.

  • Distal cholangiocarcinoma or ampullary cancer: for: progressive obstructive jaundice; against: mass centred in the pancreatic head with duct dilatation.
  • CBD stone: for: previous gallstones, epigastric pain; against: obstruction ends at a pancreatic head mass, progressive course with weight loss; no stone seen (CT can miss stones).
  • Benign post-cholecystectomy stricture: for: surgery; against: 10 years ago, mass on CT.
  • Hepatitis or drug-induced cholestasis: against: negative serology, dilated ducts.
  • Carotenaemia: against: yellow sclera, raised bilirubin.

1. Urgent referral via the pancreatic cancer optimal care pathway to a hepatobiliary and pancreatic unit with an MDT: phone the registrar and send a letter with the results.
  2. Explain to Jake and Barbara: a warning shot, then a growth in the pancreas is blocking the bile duct, very likely a cancer, and a biopsy is needed to be sure. Do not promise surgery.
  3. Team's next steps: CT chest, endoscopic ultrasound and biopsy, MDT discussion.
  4. GP care: glucose, diet, quit support, Cancer Council.

• Go to the ED, or call 000 if very unwell, for fever, shivers or shakes, worsening tummy pain, confusion or drowsiness, vomiting blood or black stools.
  • Same-day GP or ED review for a swollen or painful leg; call 000 for sudden breathlessness or chest pain.
  • See the GP sooner for persistent vomiting or being unable to eat, a bad itch, or very high sugars with thirst and passing a lot of urine.
  • Follow-up: GP review within a week. Confirm the specialist appointment date, and call the practice if he has not heard within a few days. Give written information and the Cancer Council number, and offer a family meeting with Barbara and his son.

ddx.dx: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing obstructive jaundice
ddx.for: Progressive jaundice with dark urine, pale stools, pain radiating to the back, weight loss, smoking since 15, diabetes from age 75, CA 19-9 of 1,240 and a pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign.
Progressive painless-to-mild obstructive jaundice with weight loss, a dilated CBD and a raised CA 19-9.
ddx.against: The mass is centred in the pancreatic head with pancreatic duct dilatation and body and tail atrophy.

ddx.dx: Choledocholithiasis (retained or recurrent common bile duct stone)
ddx.for: Previous gallstone disease needing cholecystectomy, and epigastric pain.
ddx.against: The obstruction ends at a pancreatic head mass and the course is progressive with weight loss; no stone is seen, though CT can miss stones.

ddx.for: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the past and a dilated common bile duct.
ddx.against: Surgery was 10 years ago and the duct ends at a pancreatic head mass.

ddx.dx: Intrahepatic cholestasis from drug-induced liver injury or viral hepatitis
ddx.for: Takes atorvastatin and a supplement, unsure of vaccination, tried cocaine when young, and the ALT is raised.
ddx.against: No new medicines, hepatitis serology negative, and dilated bile ducts on CT.

ddx.for: His wife has been giving him carrot juice.
ddx.against: Scleral icterus (carotenaemia spares the sclera), dark urine, pale stools and a bilirubin of 186.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, give examination findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Jake volunteers very little: give the pale stools only when the candidate asks about stool colour, and the radiation to the back and the pain score only when asked. If the candidate orders tests in Part 1, say the results will come in Part 2. Whatever the candidate planned, the bloods were taken on the day and the CT was done two days later. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Jake and Barbara are in the waiting room while you call the registrar; they come back in for Question 3. Jake asks his two questions once each during Question 3; the supervising GP is in the room, so the student can explain the results.

The source marked the history heavily (pain, dark urine, pale stools, systemic symptoms, PMH, medications, allergies, family and social history). Credit the Courvoisier point if the candidate notes that a palpable gallbladder cannot be expected after cholecystectomy.

A high-performing candidate asks about urine and stool colour, characterises the pain including the radiation to the back, picks up the anorexia, weight loss and lethargy, connects the recent-onset diabetes and smoking to pancreatic cancer, and examines for weight loss, Virchow's node, chronic liver disease and an abdominal mass. In Part 2 they read the cholestatic LFTs and the INR correctly, treat CA 19-9 as supportive but not diagnostic, recognise the double duct sign and the apparently resectable tumour, refer urgently, break the news honestly without promising surgery, and give clear advice about cholangitis.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history without asking about stool colour, weight or the cholecystectomy, accepts carotenaemia or hepatitis, calls the CA 19-9 diagnostic, plans routine outpatient referral, or gives no fever or rigor red flags.
explain:
Diagnosis

Jake has obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice from a suspected pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. The history points to obstruction: jaundice that has deepened over more than a month, tea-coloured urine (conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and passes into the urine) and pale stools (no bile reaching the gut). Since he has had a cholecystectomy, a common bile duct stone, stricture or intrahepatic cholestasis could cause this. However, a mild epigastric ache radiating to the back, anorexia, weight loss and lethargy in an older smoker with recent-onset diabetes point to malignancy: pancreatic head cancer or cholangiocarcinoma.

Approach to jaundice

  • Pre-hepatic (haemolysis, Gilbert's): unconjugated bilirubin, normal-coloured urine and stools.
  • Hepatic (viral, alcohol- or drug-induced hepatitis, cirrhosis): ALT and AST raised more than ALP, often with risk factors or stigmata of chronic liver disease.
  • Post-hepatic (stones, strictures, pancreatic or biliary cancer): conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT raised far more than the transaminases, dark urine, pale stools, itch, and dilated ducts on imaging.

Carotenaemia from carrot juice yellows the skin, especially the palms, but spares the sclera, and the bilirubin is normal, so it cannot explain yellow eyes. Courvoisier's law (a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in painless jaundice suggests malignancy rather than stones) does not apply after cholecystectomy.

Pancreatic cancer

Pancreatic cancer is the third most common cause of cancer death in Australia, and 5-year survival is around 13%. Surgical resection is the only potential cure. Risk factors include smoking, diabetes (new-onset diabetes in older adults can be an early sign), obesity, chronic pancreatitis and family history. Jake's HbA1c rising from 6.6% to 8.4% while he loses weight fits this.

Interpreting the results

  • LFTs: a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with ALP and GGT raised far more than ALT and AST is cholestatic.
  • INR 1.4: vitamin K is fat-soluble and needs bile to be absorbed, so obstruction prolongs the INR. Albumin is only mildly low. This matters before ERCP, EUS or surgery.
  • FBC and CRP: mild anaemia; normal white cells and a near-normal CRP in an afebrile patient argue against cholangitis now.
  • CA 19-9: a very high level supports pancreatic or biliary cancer but is not diagnostic: biliary obstruction and cholangitis raise it, and some people cannot make it. It is useful as a baseline and for follow-up.
  • Hepatitis serology: negative, excluding viral hepatitis.
  • CT pancreatic protocol: a hypoattenuating head mass with dilatation of both the bile duct and pancreatic duct (the double duct sign) is the classic appearance. Staging looks at vessel involvement (the SMA, coeliac axis, common hepatic artery, SMV and portal vein) and metastases (liver, peritoneum, lungs). Jake's tumour appears resectable on imaging. CT can miss common bile duct stones, so the absence of a stone counts for less than the mass at the point of obstruction.

The source's further investigations were FBE, UEC, LFT, lipase, hepatitis serology and CA 19-9, then a pancreatic-protocol CT of the abdomen.

Management

Suspected pancreatic cancer should be referred urgently through the optimal care pathway to a specialist hepatobiliary and pancreatic team that works within a multidisciplinary team. The GP phones the registrar, sends the results and allergy details, and stays involved. The team will usually stage with a CT of the chest, get a tissue diagnosis by endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy, and discuss surgery (a pancreaticoduodenectomy, the Whipple procedure) and chemotherapy at the MDT. Pre-operative biliary stenting by ERCP is not routine, but is used for cholangitis, troublesome itch, or when surgery is delayed (for example for neoadjuvant chemotherapy). Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is common with head tumours, and enzyme replacement is often started (Australasian Pancreatic Club). Glycaemic control, nutrition, smoking cessation, psychological support for Jake and Barbara, and advance care planning are part of GP care.

Safety netting

Fever, rigors and worsening pain in obstructive jaundice suggest acute cholangitis, an emergency needing IV antibiotics and biliary drainage (eTG); his cefazolin allergy matters for the choice. He should also seek urgent care for confusion, gastrointestinal bleeding (raised INR), persistent vomiting (duodenal obstruction) or a swollen painful leg (cancer increases the risk of venous thromboembolism), and call 000 for sudden breathlessness or chest pain. Arrange GP review within a week and check that the specialist appointment has been made.
points: Dark urine, pale stools and a cholestatic LFT pattern (conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT raised more than ALT) mean post-hepatic obstruction; always ask specifically about stool colour.
Jaundice with weight loss, anorexia and back pain in an older smoker with new-onset diabetes is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise.
Carotenaemia spares the sclera, and Courvoisier's sign cannot help after a cholecystectomy.
CA 19-9 supports but does not diagnose pancreatic cancer: biliary obstruction alone raises it. A pancreatic-protocol CT showing a head mass with a double duct sign is the key result.
Refer suspected pancreatic cancer urgently through the optimal care pathway to a specialist pancreatic MDT; surgery is the only potential cure, so delay matters.
Safety-net for cholangitis (fever, rigors, worsening pain), bleeding from a raised INR, and vomiting, and arrange early GP follow-up.
